Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is one of the most serious fungal diseases of apple trees worldwide, attacking leaves, blossoms, and developing fruit.
symptoms: Velvety olive-green to dull brown circular spots on leaf surfaces
Spots darken and turn velvety/corky with age
Leaves become distorted, puckered, yellow, and drop prematurely
Scabby, cracked lesions on apple fruit surfaces
organic_treatment: Spray copper octanoate or liquid sulfur spray during early green tip stage
Apply potassium bicarbonate (Armicarb / Kaligreen) upon first spot appearance
Use Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide as a preventative foliar spray
Remove and destroy infected fallen leaves to interrupt overwintering fungal spores
chemical_treatment: Captan 50 WP (2-2.5 kg/ha) or Mancozeb 75 WP at 7-10 day intervals during wet periods
Myclobutanil (Rally 40WSP) or Difenoconazole for systemic curative action
Dodine during pre-bloom and petal fall for high-risk orchards
prevention: Plant scab-resistant cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Freedom, Honeycrisp, Enterprise)
Prune canopy during dormancy to promote air circulation and sunlight penetration
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; keep leaf surface wetting below 6 hours
Apply 5% urea spray in autumn to speed fallen leaf decomposition
Apple___Apple_scab.favorable_weather: Cool, wet spring weather (13°C-24°C) with extended leaf wetness periods (>9 hours)

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot attacks fruit, leaves (frogeye leaf spot), and bark/twigs (cankers), causing significant yield loss and limb dieback.
symptoms: Small purple flecks enlarging into circular tan spots with dark purple margins (frogeye pattern)
Firm, dry rot on fruit with concentric dark and light rings starting near blossom end
Sunken, reddish-brown cankers on branches and limbs
Infected fruit mummifies and remains attached to twigs through winter
organic_treatment: Spray copper sulfate or Bordeaux mixture before bud break
Apply sulfur-based fungicides during early petal fall
Immediately prune out dead wood and cankered branches 15 cm below infected tissue
chemical_treatment: Thiophanate-methyl (Topsin-M) combined with Captan
Strobilurin fungicides (Flint, Pristine, Sovran) rotated to prevent resistance
Mancozeb applications from pink bud stage through mid-summer
prevention: Remove all mummified fruit, dead limbs, and fire blight strikes during winter
Sterilize pruning tools in 70% isopropyl alcohol between cuts
Control insect pests (e.g., plum curculio) that create wounds for fungal entry
Apple___Black_rot.favorable_weather: Warm temperatures (20°C-27°C) accompanied by frequent rainfall and high relative humidity

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: A fungal disease requiring both apple trees and Eastern red cedar (juniper) trees to complete its complex two-year life cycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange or reddish spots on upper surface of leaves
Tiny black pycnia appear within orange lesions
Tube-like fungal structures (aecia) protrude from leaf undersides in mid-summer
Severe infections cause defoliation and dwarfed, blemished fruit
organic_treatment: Apply sulfur dust or wettable sulfur when cedar galls are releasing orange gelatinous horns
Use Serenade Garden (Bacillus amyloliquefaciens) bio-fungicide weekly in spring
Remove nearby red cedar or juniper trees within 1-2 miles if feasible
chemical_treatment: Myclobutanil (Immunox / Rally) applied at pink bud through cover sprays
Mancozeb or Metiram from tight cluster through second cover spray
Trifloxystrobin or Azoxystrobin during peak spore discharge
prevention: Select resistant apple cultivars (e.g., Redfree, Dayton, William's Pride, Freedom)
Scout and prune gelatinous rust galls from nearby ornamental junipers in late winter
Maintain tree vigor with balanced potassium and phosphorous fertilization
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.favorable_weather: Warm, rainy spring days (12°C-24°C) with persistent moisture causing cedar galls to swell

Apple___healthy.description: The apple foliage shows clean, vibrant green pigmentation without signs of fungal lesions, bacterial blights, insect damage, or nutrient chlorosis.
symptoms: Uniform deep green color across all leaf blades
Smooth margins with characteristic fine serrations
No spots, necrotic margins, curling, or powdery residues
Strong petiole attachment and vigorous terminal shoot growth
organic_treatment: No curative action required
Maintain periodic foliar neem oil or seaweed extract for general immunity boost
Apply balanced organic compost or well-rotted manure in early spring
chemical_treatment: No chemical sprays necessary
Follow standard seasonal preventative IPM monitoring schedule
prevention: Maintain drip irrigation ensuring regular deep watering without wetting foliage
Inspect orchard weekly for early symptoms of codling moth, aphids, or scab
Prune annually in late winter for air flow and optimal sun exposure
Apple___healthy.favorable_weather: Temperate climates with moderate rainfall, adequate chilling hours in winter, and sunny summer days

Blueberry___healthy.description: Vibrant, glossy blueberry leaves displaying normal cuticle development and excellent vegetative vigor.
symptoms: Glossy, ovate deep green leaves
Absence of leaf spots, rust pustules, or stem cankers
Healthy red/brown new cane development
No signs of iron chlorosis (interveinal yellowing)
organic_treatment: No treatment required
Maintain acidic soil mulch with pine bark or pine needles
Top-dress with sulfur chips if soil pH rises above 5.2
chemical_treatment: No chemical treatment needed
Monitor soil pH (maintain 4.5-5.0) and micronutrient balance
prevention: Ensure acidic, well-draining soil rich in organic matter
Mulch 3-4 inches deep to preserve moisture and suppress weeds
Maintain regular drip irrigation; avoid high-salinity water
Blueberry___healthy.favorable_weather: Cool to moderate temperatures, acidic peat/sandy loam soils with adequate winter chill

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew is a destructive fungal disease affecting both sweet and tart cherry leaves, young shoots, and ripening fruit.
symptoms: White powdery, circular fungal patches on young expanding leaves
Upward curling, twisting, and distortion of infected leaf margins
Blistered or stunted shoot growth
Dull white mycelium covering fruit stems and cherries, leading to shriveling
organic_treatment: Spray horticultural mineral oil (JMS Stylet Oil) at early shoot elongation
Apply potassium bicarbonate (MilStop / Kaligreen) or sulfur spray
Apply bio-fungicides containing Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma
chemical_treatment: Quinoxyfen (Quintec) or Fluopyram + Trifloxystrobin (Luna Sensation)
Myclobutanil (Rally 40WSP) or Tebuconazole (Elite)
Rotate FRAC codes (3, 7, 11, 13) to prevent fungicide resistance
prevention: Prune dense canopies to maximize light penetration and wind movement
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which creates tender susceptible flushes
Begin fungicide applications at petal fall/shuck fall before epidemic onset
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.favorable_weather: Warm days (20°C-28°C) with dry conditions and high ambient humidity at night

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: Healthy cherry foliage with crisp serrated margins, rich emerald color, and clean petioles.
symptoms: Even dark green coloration across the leaf blade
Intact leaf margins free of shot-hole perforations or necrosis
No white fungal powdery coatings or bacterial gumming
Robust shoot growth and healthy leaf clustering around spurs
organic_treatment: No treatment required
Apply fish emulsion or seaweed foliar spray during shoot extension
chemical_treatment: None required
Maintain standard orchard sanitation and dormant oil sprays
prevention: Ensure proper rootstock drainage to prevent phytophthora root rot
Apply dormant copper sprays in late fall to prevent bacterial canker
Net or protect ripening fruit from birds and spotted wing drosophila
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.favorable_weather: Mild spring climates with low humidity, well-draining soils, and cool winters

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: One of the most destructive foliar diseases of maize worldwide, causing rapid leaf blighting and severe grain yield reduction.
symptoms: Small, rectangular tan to gray spots running parallel between leaf veins
Lesions enlarge to 1.5 - 6 cm long with crisp, parallel straight edges
Under high humidity, lesions develop grayish fungal sporulation
Extensive leaf blight leading to premature plant death and stalk lodging
organic_treatment: Foliar application of Bacillus subtilis or bio-sulfur at early vegetative stages
Deep tillage of crop residue to accelerate residue decomposition
Intercropping with non-host legume crops (soybeans, cowpeas)
chemical_treatment: Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole (Amistar Top) at VT/R1 growth stage
Pyraclostrobin (Headline AMP) or Picoxystrobin (Aproach)
Propiconazole (Tilt 250 EC) sprayed at first sign of disease on upper leaves
prevention: Select high-yielding corn hybrids with strong genetic tolerance to Gray Leaf Spot
Implement minimum 2-year crop rotation with non-grass crops
Manage plant population density to ensure canopy ventilation
Avoid continuous no-till corn on corn cropping systems
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.favorable_weather: Prolonged warm, humid conditions (>25°C-30°C) with persistent leaf wetness (>12 hours)

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust occurs wherever corn is grown, with airborne urediniospores blowing in from southern overwintering zones.
symptoms: Golden-brown to cinnamon-brown elongated pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the leaf epidermis, releasing powdery rusty-brown spores
Pustules turn brownish-black later in the season as teliospores develop
Severe infection causes leaf chlorosis, necrosis, and reduced ear fill
organic_treatment: Spray wettable sulfur or copper hydroxide before severe blister stage
Apply compost tea enriched with Trichoderma harzianum
Plant early in the season to mature crops before peak rust spore migration
chemical_treatment: Pyraclostrobin + Fluxapyroxad (Priaxor) applied at tasseling stage
Azoxystrobin + Propiconazole (Quilt Xcel)
Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil when pustules appear on lower leaves prior to silk
prevention: Plant corn hybrids with Rp gene-mediated resistance
Monitor sentinel rust plots and meteorological storm spore tracking
Maintain optimal nitrogen balance (avoid nitrogen excess or severe deficiency)
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.favorable_weather: Moderate temperatures (16°C-25°C) combined with high relative humidity (>95%) and night dew

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: A serious foliar fungal disease that causes rapid loss of photosynthetic leaf area when infection occurs during silking.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions (2.5 to 15 cm long)
Dark olive-green soot-like fungal spores produced in the center of damp lesions
Lesions coalesce, causing large sections of leaves to wither and burn up
Premature senescence of ear leaf and whole plant lodging
organic_treatment: Apply copper octanoate or sulfur-based formulations at V6-V8 stage
Spray bio-control agents such as Bacillus amyloliquefaciens
Shred corn stalks post-harvest to promote rapid microbial breakdown
chemical_treatment: Trifloxystrobin + Prothioconazole (Delaro 325 SC)
Azoxystrobin + Propiconazole (Stratego YLD)
Apply fungicide between VT (tasseling) and R2 (blister) if disease is present on lower canopy
prevention: Plant corn hybrids with Ht gene resistance (Ht1, Ht2, Ht3, or HtN)
Rotate with soybeans, alfalfa, or small grains for at least one year
Incorporate residue into soil with chisel plowing in high-risk zones
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.favorable_weather: Moderate temperatures (18°C-27°C) accompanied by frequent rains, heavy dew, and overcast skies

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: Vigorous, broad emerald green maize leaves showing pristine photosynthetic capability and strong midrib architecture.
symptoms: Deep, rich green leaf blades without yellowing or discoloration
Strong prominent central midrib with no lesions or pustules
Uniform stand height, strong stalk development, and clean whorls
No insect boring or armyworm feeding damage
organic_treatment: No curative action required
Side-dress with composted chicken manure or legume cover crop green manure
chemical_treatment: None required
Maintain side-dress nitrogen management based on soil nitrate test (PSNT)
prevention: Maintain optimal plant spacing (30-inch rows at 32,000 plants/acre)
Scout fields weekly during vegetative and reproductive stages
Apply timely irrigation during critical silking and grain filling phases
Corn_(maize)___healthy.favorable_weather: Warm sunny days (25°C-32°C), adequate summer rains, and fertile well-drained soils

Grape___Black_rot.description: One of the most destructive grape diseases in warm, humid regions, capable of causing 80-100% crop loss if left uncontrolled.
symptoms: Small circular reddish-brown leaf spots with thin black margins
Tiny pimple-like black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) arranged in rings inside spots
Infected berries turn light brown, soften, wrinkle, and shrivel into hard, black mummies
Cane lesions appear as sunken, dark purple to black elliptical cankers
organic_treatment: Apply Bordeaux mixture or copper soap from 1-inch shoot growth until 4 weeks post-bloom
Sulfur sprays at 7-10 day intervals (monitor phytotoxicity on sensitive cultivars)
Strict sanitation: remove all mummified grape clusters and burn or bury them
chemical_treatment: Mancozeb 75 DF or Captan 80 WDG applied from bud break through veraison
Myclobutanil (Rally 40WSP) or Tebuconazole (Elite) for powerful curative post-infection control
Azoxystrobin (Abound) or Kresoxim-methyl (Sovran)
prevention: Prune vines to open up leaf canopy for maximum sunlight and rapid drying
Cultivate or disk vineyard floor in spring to bury overwintered mummies
Plant tolerant grape varieties (e.g., Norton, Chancellor) where black rot pressure is intense
Grape___Black_rot.favorable_weather: Warm temperatures (21°C-32°C) with persistent rainfall and leaf moisture lasting 7 to 24 hours

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).pathogen: Complex of Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium minimum, and Fomitiporia mediterranea
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: A complex fungal trunk disease that damages the vascular system of mature grapevines, leading to berry measles, apoplexy, and vine death.
symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis and necrosis creating a distinctive 'tiger-stripe' pattern on leaves
Small, dark brown to purple circular spots ('measles') on berry skins
Berries crack, turn sour, and wither on the bunch
Internal trunk cross-section shows dark gummy spots and yellowish spongy wood decay (white rot)
Sudden vine wilting and collapse ('apoplexy') during hot summer spells
organic_treatment: Apply Trichoderma-based wound protectants (e.g., Vintec) onto pruning wounds immediately after cutting
Paint pruning cuts with natural pine resin or vegetable oil sealant
Remedial surgery: cut trunk below decayed necrotic zone and retrain a healthy sucker
chemical_treatment: No systemic chemical cures exist once trunk vascular tissue is colonized
Apply wound protectant fungicides (Thiophanate-methyl / Pyraclostrobin) immediately post-pruning
Sodium tetraborate / Boron sprays applied to help maintain vascular integrity
prevention: Delay winter pruning until late dormant season (sap flow helps push out fungal spores)
Double-pruning technique: preliminary machine hedge in winter, final hand cut in late spring
Avoid making large pruning wounds on old wood; disinfect shears between vines
Purchase certified virus- and pathogen-tested nursery rootstocks
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).favorable_weather: Drought stress followed by hot summer temperatures (>30°C) triggering acute apoplectic collapse

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Late-season foliar disease causing significant premature leaf defoliation, weakening the vine for the following season.
symptoms: Irregular brown necrotic lesions surrounded by a prominent yellowish chlorotic halo
Velvety, dark sooty olivaceous fungal growth on the underside of lesions
Leaves become brittle, curl up, and fall off prematurely before harvest
Weak cane maturity and poor winter hardiness
organic_treatment: Copper oxychloride or copper hydroxide sprays applied post-flowering
Wettable sulfur foliar sprays during canopy development
Neem oil 1% spray every 10-14 days to reduce fungal sporulation
chemical_treatment: Mancozeb 75 WP (2 g/L) or Chlorothalonil 75 WP
Difenoconazole 25 EC or Carbendazim 50 WP
Post-harvest protective spray with Bordeaux mixture (1%)
prevention: Shoot positioning and leaf removal around fruiting zone to facilitate aeration
Rake and compost or destroy dropped infected leaves post-harvest
Avoid excessive overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation systems
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.favorable_weather: Humid tropical and subtropical vineyard regions with frequent monsoon showers (24°C-30°C)

Grape___healthy.description: Vibrant, broad, palmate grapevine leaves exhibiting robust photosynthesis, clean petioles, and healthy tendril development.
symptoms: Deep green uniform lamina without interveinal mottling or spots
Flexible, crisp leaves with clean defined lobes and serrated margins
No powdery white fungal films, berry mummies, or cane cankers
Active shoot tip elongation and strong vine vigor
organic_treatment: No curative action required
Foliar application of seaweed kelp extract and micronutrient zinc-iron spray
chemical_treatment: None required
Maintain preventative dormant sulfur/oil sprays as per local viticulture guidelines
prevention: Implement vertical shoot positioning (VSP) trellis for balanced sunlight
Maintain balanced vine nutrition avoiding excess nitrogen that causes dense canopies
Manage vineyard cover crops to regulate soil moisture and beneficial insect habitats
Grape___healthy.favorable_weather: Mediterranean and sunny temperate climates with warm dry summers and cool wet winters

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: The most destructive citrus disease on earth, vectored by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri). It clogs the phloem, starving the roots and killing trees within 3-5 years.
symptoms: Asymmetric 'blotchy mottle' yellowing pattern across leaf veins (one half yellow, one half green)
Thickened, corky, yellow veins resembling severe nutrient deficiency (zinc/manganese)
Small, hard, lopsided fruit that fails to color properly, remaining green at stylar end ('greening')
Bitter, salty, acidic juice with aborted dark seeds
Twig dieback, premature fruit drop, and general tree decline
organic_treatment: No cure exists once infected; mandatory removal of diseased trees to protect orchard
Bio-control of vector: release Tamarixia radiata parasitoid wasps against Asian citrus psyllids
Apply high-potency nutritional foliar cocktails (zinc, manganese, potassium, iron, phosphites) to prolong tree production
chemical_treatment: Vector control is paramount: Imidacloprid, Thiamethoxam, or Clothianidin systemic drenches
Foliar pyrethroid sprays (Beta-cyfluthrin) or organophosphates during leaf flushing
Trunk injection of oxytetracycline hydrochloride (OTC) where approved by regulatory authorities
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free nursery stock produced under insect-proof screenhouses
Eradicate and burn infected trees immediately upon positive molecular PCR test
Scout young flush shoots weekly for psyllid eggs, nymphs, and white waxy excretions
Adhere strictly to regional citrus quarantine zones and transit restrictions
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).favorable_weather: Subtropical and tropical climates where Asian citrus psyllids breed year-round (20°C-32°C)

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: A serious bacterial disease attacking leaves, twigs, and fruit of peaches, nectarines, and plums, causing extensive defoliation and fruit culling.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple to dark brown
Infected spot centers drop out, leaving a ragged 'shot-hole' appearance
Tips of leaves yellow and drop prematurely, causing severe summer defoliation
Deep, pitted, crater-like cracked lesions with gummy bacterial ooze on peach fruit
organic_treatment: Spray copper octanoate or copper hydroxide during dormant and bud-swell stages
Apply Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or Serenade bio-fungicide during early cover sprays
Plant windbreaks to prevent blowing sand and soil abrasion that creates entry wounds
chemical_treatment: Oxytetracycline (Mycoshield / FlameOut) applied during bloom through shuck split
Low-rate copper compounds (Kocide 3000) applied at 7-day intervals post-bloom (caution for phytotoxicity)
Zinc sulfate + lime foliar sprays
prevention: Plant resistant peach cultivars (e.g., Bounty, Candor, Harrow Diamond, Redhaven)
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which produces succulent, highly vulnerable shoots
Prune to promote airflow and speed up canopy drying times
Peach___Bacterial_spot.favorable_weather: Warm (21°C-28°C), wet, windy spring weather with blowing rains and sandy abrasive soils

Peach___healthy.description: Vibrant, spear-shaped lanceolate peach leaves showing lush green coloration, crisp margins, and strong shoot vigor.
symptoms: Even bright green color with shiny upper cuticle
Smooth margins free of shot-hole perforations or water-soaked lesions
No leaf curl, distortion, yellowing, or gumming along petioles
Strong terminal extension and healthy peach fruitlet development
organic_treatment: No curative action required
Apply sea kelp extract or mild compost tea to maintain foliar vigor
chemical_treatment: None required
Follow standard dormant copper sprays for Peach Leaf Curl prevention
prevention: Thin heavy fruit sets early to balance branch load and tree energy
Paint lower tree trunks with white latex paint to prevent winter sunscald and borers
Maintain 3-4 inches of mulch around drip line, avoiding direct contact with trunk bark
Peach___healthy.favorable_weather: Sunny, warm climates with moderate summer humidity and sufficient winter chill hours

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: One of the most devastating pepper diseases, resulting in rapid defoliation, sunburned fruit, and unmarketable spotted peppers.
symptoms: Small, circular to irregular water-soaked spots on leaf undersides
Spots turn purplish-brown to black with pale brownish centers
Leaves turn yellow around spots and drop rapidly, leaving bare stems
Raised, rough, blister-like or scabby brown spots on green and red bell peppers
organic_treatment: Apply copper octanoate (copper soap) or fixed copper fungicides every 7-10 days
Spray Regalia (Reynoutria sachalinensis extract) to induce systemic plant resistance
Apply bacteriophage products (AgriPhage) specific to Xanthomonas strains
chemical_treatment: Fixed copper (Kocide / Champion) tank-mixed with Mancozeb (improves copper solubility and bactericidal kill)
Acibenzolar-S-methyl (Actigard) plant defense activator applied early in vegetative stage
Streptomycin (in greenhouse transplants only, prior to field setting)
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seeds and disease-resistant bell pepper hybrids (races 1-10)
Hot water seed treatment (50°C for 25 minutes) before planting
Never work in pepper fields while leaves are wet with dew or rain
Rotate fields away from solanaceous crops (tomatoes, peppers, eggplants) for at least 2-3 years
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.favorable_weather: Hot, humid, rainy weather (24°C-30°C) with splashing rain and wind-driven storms

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: Lush, glossy, deep green bell pepper foliage with strong apical branching, pristine leaf blades, and vigorous flower sets.
symptoms: Broad, vibrant, glossy green leaves without chlorosis or curling
Clean leaf undersides without water-soaked lesions or bacterial spots
Healthy white flower blossoms and firm, glossy green bell fruitlets
Strong, upright central stems with robust branching
organic_treatment: No curative action required
Apply liquid seaweed or fish hydrolysate every 2-3 weeks for micronutrient support
chemical_treatment: None required
Maintain calcium and magnesium supplementation to prevent blossom end rot
prevention: Maintain consistent soil moisture using drip irrigation and plastic or straw mulch
Stake or cage pepper plants to support heavy fruit loads and keep leaves off soil
Monitor for aphids, thrips, and mites that transmit plant viruses
Pepper,_bell___healthy.favorable_weather: Warm days (21°C-29°C), mild nights (16°C-20°C), and well-drained loamy soils rich in organic matter

Potato___Early_blight.description: A common and destructive fungal foliage and tuber disease that attacks older leaves first and progresses upward as the crop matures.
symptoms: Dark brown to black oval or angular spots appearing on older lower leaves
Characteristic concentric rings producing a 'target-board' or 'bullseye' pattern
Yellow chlorotic halo surrounding lesions as fungal toxins spread
Leaves turn completely yellow, wither, and drop; sunken dark corky lesions on tubers
organic_treatment: Spray copper sulfate / copper hydroxide at 7-10 day intervals
Apply Bacillus subtilis (Serenade ASO) or bio-sulfur
Maintain high plant vigor with balanced nitrogen; stressed plants are far more susceptible
chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil (Bravo Weather Stik) or Mancozeb (Dithane M-45) preventative protectants
Azoxystrobin (Quadris) or Pyraclostrobin (Headline)
Boscalid (Endura) or Difenoconazole (Revus Top) for curative systemic protection
prevention: Practice a 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (cereals, legumes, corn)
Plant certified disease-free seed tubers with high vigor
Use drip or furrow irrigation to minimize canopy moisture; irrigate in early morning
Destroy and plow under vine residues immediately after harvest
Potato___Early_blight.favorable_weather: Alternating wet and dry periods with warm temperatures (24°C-29°C) and heavy night dew

Potato___Late_blight.description: The notorious organism responsible for the Irish Potato Famine. Late blight can destroy entire potato fields within a few days under conducive cool, wet conditions.
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked pale-to-dark olive-green lesions on leaves and stems
Lesions rapidly enlarge and turn dark brown to purplish-black with a pale green border
Delicate, white cottony mildew growth on leaf undersides in humid conditions
Stems develop dark brown cankers, causing rapid foliage collapse and a foul odor
Tubers show brown to purplish sunken surface rot and internal granular dry rot
organic_treatment: Apply Bordeaux mixture or copper octanoate continuously every 5-7 days before disease onset
Once infection takes hold in fields, immediate vine killing (desiccation) to save tubers
Destroy and bury all infected plant material; do not compost late blight vines
chemical_treatment: Mandipropamid (Revus) or Cyazofamid (Ranman) - highly effective oomycete specifics
Fluopicolide (Presidio) or Mefenoxam / Metalaxyl (Ridomil Gold - check for resistance)
Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb as multi-site protectant tank-mix partners
prevention: Plant certified seed potatoes free of late blight inoculum
Eliminate cull piles, volunteer potato plants, and rogue infected plants immediately
Monitor regional Late Blight Decision Support Systems (DSS) and weather alerts
Ensure proper hilling of potato rows to create a soil barrier preventing spore wash onto tubers
Potato___Late_blight.favorable_weather: Cool, overcast, wet weather (10°C-21°C) with relative humidity near 100% and rainfall

Potato___healthy.description: Dense, vigorous dark green potato canopy actively photosynthesizing and directing starch storage to underground developing tubers.
symptoms: Lush, compound dark green leaves with crisp leaflet edges
Sturdy upright stems without dark necrotic lesions or soft rot
Abundant flowering and vigorous canopy closure across rows
No wilting, target spots, or white fungal downy sporulation
organic_treatment: No curative action required
Foliar spray of seaweed extract and humic acid to promote tuber bulking
chemical_treatment: None required
Continue routine preventative fungicide spray program in high blight risk areas
prevention: Hill soil around plant bases to prevent greening of developing tubers and tuber blight
Maintain consistent soil moisture (approx. 70-80% field capacity during tuber bulking)
Scout lower leaves and field edges weekly for early signs of Colorado potato beetle and blight
Potato___healthy.favorable_weather: Mild sunny days (18°C-24°C) with cool nights and well-drained sandy loam soil

Raspberry___healthy.description: Healthy raspberry foliage showing compound serrated leaves, silvery-green undersides, and vigorous cane shoots.
symptoms: Compound leaves with 3-5 ovate, sharply toothed deep green leaflets
Clean, silvery-white pubescence on leaf undersides
Sturdy primocanes and floricanes free of spur blight lesions or anthracnose spots
No yellow mosaic, curling, or cane gall tumors
organic_treatment: No curative action required
Apply pine bark or wood chip mulch to preserve moisture and suppress weeds
chemical_treatment: None required
Maintain preventative dormant lime sulfur sprays prior to spring bud break
prevention: Trellis canes to maintain upright growth and promote airflow
Prune spent floricanes to ground level immediately following summer harvest
Plant in raised beds or berms to prevent Phytophthora root rot in heavy soils
Raspberry___healthy.favorable_weather: Cool to moderate temperate climates, well-draining soils with ample organic matter

Soybean___healthy.description: Uniform trifoliate soybean leaves with rich chlorophyll content, active nitrogen-fixing root nodules, and clean pods.
symptoms: Trifoliate leaves exhibiting uniform bright emerald green color
Intact leaf lamina free of frogeye spots, rust pustules, or sudden death syndrome chlorosis
Strong main stem with dense pod clusters along nodes
Active nitrogen fixation indicated by pink internal root nodule color
organic_treatment: No treatment required
Apply foliar micronutrient spray (molybdenum, manganese) during early flowering (R1)
chemical_treatment: None required
Follow IPM economic threshold scouting for bean leaf beetles and stinkbugs
prevention: Inoculate seeds with Bradyrhizobium japonicum before planting in new fields
Implement minimum 2-year crop rotation with corn or small grains
Maintain weed canopy control to avoid pest reservoirs and disease microclimates
Soybean___healthy.favorable_weather: Warm growing season (21°C-30°C) with evenly distributed rainfall during flowering and pod fill

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: The most common and destructive foliage disease of cucurbits, causing rapid leaf yellowing, sunscald of exposed fruit, and yield loss.
symptoms: Distinct white talcum-powder-like circular fungal spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces
Powdery patches expand to cover the entire leaf blade and petiole
Infected leaves turn yellow, then brown, becoming brittle and crisp like parchment paper
Premature defoliation exposing squash fruit to sunburn and reducing sugar content
organic_treatment: Spray potassium bicarbonate (MilStop / GreenCure) at 3 g/L at first sign of white spots
Apply 0.5-1% neem oil or horticultural oil spray weekly (spray in early morning/evening)
Dilute milk spray (40% whole milk / 60% water) exposed to sunlight generates antiseptic free radicals
Foliar application of Bacillus amyloliquefaciens (Double Nickel / Serenade)
chemical_treatment: Triflumizole (Procure) or Myclobutanil (Rally 40WSP)
Cyflufenamid (Torino) or Penthiopyrad (Fontelis)
Rotate chemical modes of action every application to prevent rapid fungal resistance
prevention: Plant powdery mildew resistant squash cultivars (e.g., Success PM, Dunja, Tigress)
Space plants generously (4-6 feet between rows) to promote wind circulation and drying
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; always use drip tape underneath plastic mulch
Remove and discard heavily infected older leaves from plant bases
Squash___Powdery_mildew.favorable_weather: Warm (20°C-28°C), dry, shaded conditions with high relative humidity (>70%) at night

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: A destructive foliar disease of cultivated strawberries that weakens runner plants, dwarfs crowns, and reduces berry yields.
symptoms: Numerous small, irregular purple to dark purplish-brown spots on upper leaf surfaces
Spots remain uniformly purple or dark brown without a white center (distinguishing it from common leaf spot)
Spots coalesce causing the leaf blade to look scorched, burned, and curled upward at margins
Lesions on calyx (cap) turn brown, rendering strawberries unmarketable
organic_treatment: Spray liquid copper or copper octanoate post-harvest and in early spring
Apply bio-fungicides containing Trichoderma or Bacillus subtilis
Mow and destroy diseased foliage in renovated strawberry beds immediately after harvest
chemical_treatment: Captan 80 WDG or Thiram 24/7 applied at 10-14 day intervals
Pyraclostrobin + Boscalid (Pristine) or Cyprodinil + Fludioxonil (Switch)
Myclobutanil (Rally) applied during pre-bloom and runner formation
prevention: Plant certified disease-free, vigorous runner crowns from accredited nurseries
Choose resistant strawberry varieties (e.g., Allstar, Earliglow, Tribute, Tristar)
Maintain narrow matted rows (12-18 inches wide) to promote rapid foliage drying
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; keep mulch fresh (clean straw or pine needles)
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.favorable_weather: Warm, wet weather (20°C-26°C) with persistent moisture and splashing rains

Strawberry___healthy.description: Compact, vigorous strawberry crowns with glossy trifoliate leaves, clean flower trusses, and robust runner development.
symptoms: Glossy, deep green trifoliate leaflets with sharp serrations
Clean petioles without dark necrotic girdling lesions
Healthy white flower petals surrounding bright yellow centers
Firm, green-to-ruby red fruit developing without mildew or botrytis gray mold
organic_treatment: No curative action required
Foliar application of liquid bone meal and seaweed for flower and fruit development
chemical_treatment: None required
Maintain standard preventative strawberry IPM scouting
prevention: Mulch beds with clean wheat straw or black plastic mulch to keep fruit clean
Provide 1 to 1.5 inches of water weekly using targeted drip tape
Renovate June-bearing beds annually after harvest by thinning and weeding
Strawberry___healthy.favorable_weather: Mild sunny weather (15°C-24°C), sandy loam soils high in organic matter, pH 5.5-6.5

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: A major worldwide bacterial disease of tomatoes that causes severe leaf blighting, blossom drop, and unmarketable fruit lesions.
symptoms: Small (less than 3 mm), dark brown to black circular or angular water-soaked leaf spots
Spots often have a yellow chlorotic halo and may coalesce, causing leaf blighting
Infected leaves turn brown, wither, and drop, exposing developing tomatoes to sunscald
Small, raised, scab-like black spots with rough margins on green fruit
organic_treatment: Copper hydroxide or copper soap applied every 5-7 days during warm, wet periods
Biological control: apply AgriPhage (bacteriophage targeted to Xanthomonas)
Foliar application of Regalia (knotweed extract) to boost plant defense pathways
Remove severely infected plants to prevent field-wide bacterial contagion
chemical_treatment: Fixed copper tank-mixed with Mancozeb (greatly boosts copper efficacy against resistant strains)
Actigard (Acibenzolar-S-methyl) systemic acquired resistance inducer applied every 7-10 days
Streptomycin used only in transplant greenhouses prior to field planting
prevention: Use certified disease-free, hot-water treated seeds (50°C for 25 minutes)
Implement a 2-3 year crop rotation away from solanaceous plants (potatoes, peppers, eggplants)
Never prune, stake, or harvest plants while foliage is wet with rain or dew
Use drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers to prevent bacterial splash dispersal
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.favorable_weather: Warm (24°C-30°C), humid weather with frequent rainstorms, heavy morning dew, and splashing water

Tomato___Early_blight.description: One of the most common and persistent diseases of tomatoes, affecting foliage, stems, and fruit throughout the growing season.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots on older lower leaves, characterized by concentric rings ('target-board' or 'bullseye' appearance)
Yellow halo surrounding the circular lesions
Leaves turn completely yellow, dry up, and drop, progressing from bottom to top of plant
Dark, sunken, leathery lesions at the stem end of tomato fruit
organic_treatment: Prune away lower infected leaves up to 18 inches above soil to prevent soil-splash reinfection
Apply copper octanoate (copper soap) or fixed copper fungicides at 7-day intervals
Spray bio-fungicides containing Bacillus subtilis (Serenade) or Trichoderma harzianum
Thoroughly mulch soil with clean straw or plastic mulch to create a barrier against soil spores
chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil (Bravo / Daconil) or Mancozeb as standard multi-site protective sprays
Azoxystrobin (Quadris) or Pyraclostrobin (Cabrio)
Difenoconazole + Cyprodinil (Inspire Super) for systemic eradicant activity
prevention: Choose resistant or tolerant tomato varieties (e.g., Mountain Supreme, Defiant, Jasper)
Practice 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
Stake and cage tomato plants for upright growth and good air circulation
Water exclusively at soil level using soaker hoses or drip irrigation
Tomato___Early_blight.favorable_weather: Warm temperatures (24°C-29°C) with alternating wet periods (dew, rain) and sunny dry spells

Tomato___Late_blight.description: An aggressive, fast-moving disease that can destroy entire tomato crops and spread rapidly across neighboring farms within days.
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked pale-to-dark olive green or oily lesions on leaves
Lesions turn purplish-brown and dry out rapidly under dry conditions
White, delicate cottony fungal-like sporulation on the underside of leaves during high humidity
Stems develop greasy dark brown lesions, becoming brittle and collapsing
Fruit develops large, firm, greasy golden-brown to dark bronze leathery patches
organic_treatment: Apply fixed copper or Bordeaux mixture immediately before anticipated cool wet weather
Once infection is confirmed in garden/field, immediately bag and destroy infected plants
Do NOT compost late blight plants; dispose in sealed trash bags or bury deeply
chemical_treatment: Mandipropamid (Revus) or Cyazofamid (Ranman) - highly effective oomycete specifics
Fluopicolide (Presidio) or Propamocarb (Previcur Flex)
Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb tank-mix protectants applied every 5-7 days under high disease pressure
prevention: Plant late blight-resistant cultivars (e.g., Mountain Magic, Iron Lady, Defiant PHR, Plum Regal)
Scout plants daily during cool, overcast, damp periods
Destroy volunteer potatoes and nightshade weeds near tomato fields
Provide wide plant spacing and plant tomatoes in the sunniest, breeziest spot
Tomato___Late_blight.favorable_weather: Cool, damp, foggy, or rainy weather (12°C-22°C) with persistent relative humidity above 90%

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.pathogen: Passalora fulva (Syn. Fulvia fulva / Cladosporium fulvum) (Fungus)
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: A prevalent fungal disease particularly devastating in greenhouses, high tunnels, and unventilated polytunnels.
symptoms: Pale green to yellowish spots with indistinct margins on upper leaf surfaces
Dense, olive-green to grayish-purple velvety fungal patches on corresponding leaf undersides
Infected leaves wither, turn yellow-brown, and die prematurely
Blossoms and small fruit may abort; plants become prematurely defoliated
organic_treatment: Drastically increase ventilation: open greenhouse vents, run horizontal airflow fans
Spray copper soap or sulfur vapor (monitor temperature to avoid leaf burn)
Apply bio-fungicides like Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or Reynoutria extract
chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil 720 SC or Mancozeb 75 WG
Difenoconazole (Inspire) or Cyprodinil + Fludioxonil (Switch)
Azoxystrobin or Trifloxystrobin applied at first symptom on lower canopy
prevention: Plant resistant tomato hybrids carrying Cf resistance genes (Cf-2, Cf-4, Cf-9)
Maintain relative humidity below 85% in greenhouses through heating and air exchange
Prune suckers and lower foliage to maximize air velocity through plant canopy
Avoid wetting leaves when irrigating
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.favorable_weather: High relative humidity (>85%) and moderate temperatures (21°C-24°C) with poor ventilation

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: One of the most destructive foliage diseases of field tomatoes, causing progressive defoliation from ground level upward.
symptoms: Numerous small (1.5 - 3 mm), circular spots with dark brown margins and sunken grayish-white centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia fruiting bodies) clearly visible inside grey centers
Leaves turn completely yellow, wither, curl up, and drop
Severe lower canopy defoliation leaves fruit vulnerable to sunscald, but fruit itself is rarely infected directly
organic_treatment: Prune and remove infected lower leaves as soon as first spots appear
Apply copper hydroxide or copper soap spray every 7 days
Spray bio-fungicides containing Bacillus subtilis or Streptomyces lydicus (Actinovate)
Apply thick layer of organic mulch (straw, paper, compost) under plants
chemical_treatment: Chlorothalonil (Daconil / Bravo) applied on a 7-10 day preventative schedule
Mancozeb (Dithane M-45) or Pyraclostrobin (Cabrio)
Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole (Quadris Top)
prevention: Rotate out of solanaceous crops for a minimum of 2 full years
Stake, cage, and trellis tomatoes to keep leaves completely off the soil
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; water with drip tape early in the day
Destroy and till under all crop residue at the conclusion of harvest
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.favorable_weather: Extended wet weather with moderate temperatures (20°C-26°C) and heavy morning dews

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Microscopic sap-feeding arachnid pests that multiply exponentially in hot, dry, dusty conditions, causing severe stippling and webbing.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white speckled stippling on upper leaf surfaces
Leaves take on a bronze, bleached, or dusty appearance and dry out
Delicate, silky webbing spun across leaf undersides, petioles, and growing tips
Severe infestation causes total leaf drop, stunted plant growth, and plant death
organic_treatment: Spray insecticidal soap (potassium salts of fatty acids) thoroughly targeting leaf undersides
Apply cold-pressed pure neem oil (0.5-1%) or rosemary essential oil miticides
Release predatory mites: Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus
Blast plant undersides with strong stream of water to knock down populations and destroy webbing
chemical_treatment: Bifenazate (Acramite 50WS) - targeted mite-specific ovicide/adulticide
Abamectin (Agri-Mek) translaminar miticide
Spiromesifen (Oberon) or Etoxazole (Zeal); rotate chemical classes to avoid resistance
prevention: Avoid over-application of broad-spectrum pyrethroid insecticides that wipe out natural mite predators
Keep field borders, greenhouse paths, and headlands watered to minimize dusty conditions
Provide adequate irrigation; drought-stressed tomatoes are prime targets for rapid mite reproduction
Regularly scout leaf undersides with a 10x-20x hand lens
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.favorable_weather: Hot (>30°C), dry, dusty summer conditions with low relative humidity (<40%)

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: A fungal disease affecting leaves, stems, and fruit of tomatoes, common in warm, humid and tropical production regions.
symptoms: Pinpoint brown spots on leaves that enlarge up to 1 cm with subtle concentric rings ('target pattern')
Lesions lack the pronounced chlorotic yellow halo typical of early blight
Severely spotted leaves turn brown, wither, and drop, causing extensive defoliation
Deep, sunken, circular brown pits on fruit that may crack open
organic_treatment: Apply copper octanoate or copper hydroxide spray at 7-day intervals
Spray Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or bio-sulfur
Improve air drainage by pruning lower suckers and leaves
chemical_treatment: Fluxapyroxad + Pyraclostrobin (Priaxor) or Boscalid (Endura)
Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb as preventative protective baseline
Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole (Quadris Top)
prevention: Maintain adequate plant spacing to allow fast canopy drying
Avoid overhead irrigation; utilize drip irrigation systems
Disinfect greenhouse stakes, strings, and cages between seasons
Rotate crops away from tomatoes, peppers, soybeans, and papayas
Tomato___Target_Spot.favorable_weather: Warm, humid weather (20°C-28°C) with persistent leaf moisture lasting 12 hours or more

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.pathogen: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (Begomovirus / Geminiviridae)
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A devastating plant virus transmitted by the sweetpotato/silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Infected young plants rarely produce harvestable fruit.
symptoms: Marked upward curling and cupping of leaflet margins
Interveinal chlorosis and bright yellowing of young leaves and shoots
Severe stunting and erect bushy dwarf growth habit ('bonsai-like' appearance)
Leaflets become small, thickened, and puckered
Flower blossoms drop prematurely; fruit set is drastically reduced or absent
organic_treatment: No chemical or organic cure exists once a plant is infected with the virus
Immediately rogue out and destroy infected plants in sealed plastic bags
Control vector whiteflies with insecticidal soap, Beauveria bassiana fungus, or yellow sticky cards
Cover crops with 50-mesh insect exclusion netting during transplant stage
chemical_treatment: Control whitefly vectors: Thiamethoxam (Actara) or Imidacloprid systemic soil drench
Spirotetramat (Movento) or Pyriproxyfen (Knack) insect growth regulators
Cyantraniliprole (Verimark / Exirel) for fast feeding cessation of whiteflies
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant or tolerant tomato hybrids (carrying Ty-1, Ty-2, or Ty-3 resistance genes)
Use UV-reflective silver or aluminum mulches to repel incoming whiteflies
Maintain a 6-8 week host-free fallow period between tomato crop cycles
Eradicate weed reservoirs (e.g., Solanum nigrum, Malva, Datura) around crop perimeters
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.favorable_weather: Warm, dry climates (25°C-35°C) that favor high whitefly breeding and population explosions

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: An exceptionally stable and highly contagious mechanically transmitted plant virus that persists in plant sap, seeds, soil, and tools for years.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottling, blistering, and mosaic pattern on leaves
Leaves become distorted, fern-like, curled, or narrowed into 'shoestrings'
Plants are stunted with yellowish pale canopy
Uneven fruit ripening, internal brown necrosis in fruit flesh ('brown wall')
organic_treatment: No chemical cure exists for infected plants; rogue and destroy infected vines immediately
Workers should wash hands and dip tools in non-fat dry milk solution (20% reconstituted dry milk) which denatures the virus capsid
Do NOT smoke or use tobacco products near tomato plants (tobacco mosaic virus cross-infection)
chemical_treatment: No viricidal chemical exists for plant use
Disinfect all stakes, pruning shears, wire, and greenhouse benches with 10% household bleach or Virkon S
prevention: Plant certified virus-free seeds treated with trisodium phosphate (TSP) or dry heat
Select resistant tomato cultivars carrying Tm-1, Tm-2, or Tm-2^2 resistance genes
Sanitize pruning tools between every plant or row
Control root nematodes which can facilitate viral entry through root wounds
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.favorable_weather: Occurs under any weather condition; spreads rapidly through human handling, pruning, and grafting

Tomato___healthy.description: Lush, fragrant, deep green tomato foliage with robust branching, healthy flower trusses, and pristine fruit development.
symptoms: Even, deep forest green foliage with characteristic glandular pubescence
No chlorotic halos, brown concentric rings, or water-soaked spots
Clean, sturdy stems without black cankers or vascular browning
Vigorous blossoming and uniform green developing tomato clusters
organic_treatment: No curative action required
Foliar spray of fish and kelp emulsion every 14 days during active growth
chemical_treatment: None required
Maintain preventative calcium nitrate nutrition to prevent blossom end rot
prevention: Stake, cage, or prune into single or double leaders for optimal sunlight exposure
Maintain 2-3 inches of organic mulch to regulate soil moisture and temperature
Water deeply at soil level; avoid wetting leaves
Tomato___healthy.favorable_weather: Sunny, warm days (21°C-28°C), mild nights (15°C-18°C), and well-drained fertile loam (pH 6.2-6.8)
